848852 -- prove two things, corresponding to the two ways in which `Ev n` could have

850--- property must hold of `0`. If it was constructed by `Ev.ev_succ_succ`, then
851--- the evidence of `Ev n` is of the form `Ev.ev_succ_succ n' h'`, where
853+-- been constructed. If it was constructed by `ev_0`, then `n=0` and the

855+-- the evidence of `Ev n` is of the form `ev_succ_succ n' E'`, where
852856 -- `n = n' + 2` and `h'` is evidence for `Ev n'`. In this case, the inductive
853857 -- hypothesis says that the property we are trying to prove holds for `n'`.

1120--- will replace instances of `m` with `m' + 1`. Doing `inversion h` will

1125+-- Doing `cases h` will generate two cases. In the first case, `e1 = e2`, and
1126+-- it will replace instances of `e2` with `e1` in the goal and context. In the
1127+-- second case, `e2 = n' + 1` for some `n'` for which `le e1 n'` holds, and it
1128+-- will replace instances of `e2` with `n' + 1`. Doing `inversion h` will
11211129 -- remove impossible cases and add generated equalities to the context for
11221130 -- further use. Doing `induction h` will, in the second case, add the

517+-- ### Aside: Using Code Actions to Generate Match Skeletons
518+
519+-- Lean's language server can suggest *code actions*, which are small editor
520+-- commands that modify the source code. In VS Code, a lightbulb icon appears
521+-- on the left when a code action is available at your cursor. You can click
522+-- the icon or open the code action menu with `Ctrl + .` on Windows/Linux or
523+-- `Command + .` on macOS. For more information, see the [Lean 4 VSCode
524+-- extension
525+-- manual](https://github.com/leanprover/vscode-lean4/blob/master/vscode-lean4/manual/manual.md#code-actions).
526+
527+-- Some code actions can generate the explicit branches needed for pattern
528+-- matching. This is especially useful when working with `match` expressions,
529+-- or with tactics such as `cases` and `induction`, which we saw in previous
530+-- chapters.
531+
532+-- Let's look at an example using `induction`. For example, suppose we start
533+-- with the following incomplete proof:
534+
535+sf_expect_failure
536+  example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
537+    induction n
538+
539+-- Put your cursor on `induction n` and open the code action menu. You should
540+-- see "Generate an explicit pattern match for 'induction'." in the list. If
541+-- you choose this action, Lean adds an explicit branch for each constructor:
542+
543+example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
544+  induction n with
545+  | zero => sorry
546+  | succ n _ => sorry
547+
548+-- This gives us basic structure of the proof without requiring us to write
549+-- each branch by hand. We can then focus on proving each case.
550+
551+-- One possible proof is:
552+
553+example (n : Nat) : Nat.beq n n := by
554+  induction n with
555+  | zero => exact (beq_self zero)
556+  | succ n ih => rw [Nat.beq, ih]
557+
558+-- Note that Lean used `_` for the induction hypothesis in the generated
559+-- `succ` branch. At that point, Lean didn't know whether the unfinished proof
560+-- would need to refer to the hypothesis. Since we use it in `rw`, we replace
561+-- `_` with the name `ih`.
562+
563+-- In later chapters, we will see some tactics that can make such inaccessible
564+-- names available again.
565+
566+-- The same trick also works for `match` expressions. For example, suppose we
567+-- start with
568+
569+sf_expect_failure
570+  def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
571+    match n
572+
573+-- Lean can generate the missing branches:
574+
575+sf_expect_failure
576+  def isZero (n : Nat) : Bool :=
577+    match n with
578+    | 0 => _
579+    | n + 1 => _
580+
581+-- You can use code actions freely to fill out `induction`, `case`, and
582+-- `match` branches in this book.
583+

516589 -- `rewrite [← h]` or `rw [← h]`, where `←` is entered as `\l` or `\<-`.

2428 -- ## The `apply` Tactic
2529 
2630 -- We often encounter situations where the goal to be proved is *exactly* the
2731 -- same as some hypothesis in the context or some previously proved lemma.
2832 
29--- The `apply` tactic is useful when the goal is instead the conclusion of an
30--- implication.
31-
32--- For example, suppose we have a hypothesis `h : p → q` and our goal is `q`.
33--- We can use `apply h` to replace the goal `q` with the premise `p`:
34-
35-example (p q : Prop) (h : p → q) (hp : p) : q := by
36-  apply h
37-  exact hp
38-
39--- The `apply` tactic also works with hypotheses and lemmas whose types are
40--- implications. If the conclusion of the implication matches the current
41--- goal, its premises become new subgoals to be proved.
42-
43-example (n m o p : Nat) (hnm : n = m) (h : n = m → [n, o] = [m, p]) :
33+theorem silly1 (n m : Nat) : n = m → n = m := by
34+  intro eq
35+  /- Here, we could finish with `rw [eq]` as we
36+    have done several times before.  Or we can finish
37+    by using `apply`: -/
38+  apply eq
39+
40+-- The `apply` tactic also works with *conditional* hypotheses and lemmas: if
41+-- the statement being applied is an implication, then the premises of this
42+-- implication will be added to the list of subgoals needing to be proved.
43+
44+theorem silly2 (n m o p : Nat) :
45+    n = m →
46+    (n = m → [n, o] = [m, p]) →
4447     [n, o] = [m, p] := by
45-  apply h
46-  exact hnm
47-
48--- When we use `apply h`, Lean tries to match the conclusion of the type of
49--- `h` with the current goal. Here `h : n = m → [n, o] = [m, p]` has
50--- conclusion `[n, o] = [m, p]`, which matches the current goal. Lean then
51--- replaces the goal with the premise that is still needed, `n = m`. Then we
52--- close the goal with `exact hnm`.
53-
54--- More generally, the type of a theorem or hypothesis used with `apply` may
55--- have universally quantified variables and premises. Lean tries to match its
56--- conclusion with the current goal to determine appropriate values for the
57--- quantified variables.
58-
59-example (n m : Nat) (h₁ : (n, n) = (m, m))
60-    (h₂ : ∀ (q r : Nat), (q, q) = (r, r) → [q] = [r]) :
48+  intro eq1 eq2
49+  apply eq2
50+  apply eq1

52+-- Typically, when we use `apply h`, the statement `h` will begin with a
53+-- `forall` that introduces some *universally quantified variables*.
54+
55+-- When Lean matches the current goal against the conclusion of `h`, it will
56+-- try to find appropriate values for these variables. For example, when we do
57+-- `apply eq2` in the following proof, the universal variable `q` in `eq2`
58+-- gets instantiated with `n`, and `r` gets instantiated with `m`.
59+

61+    (n, n) = (m, m)  →
62+    (∀ (q r : Nat), (q, q) = (r, r) → [q] = [r]) →
6163     [n] = [m] := by

540+-- ## Using Tactics on Hypotheses
541+
542+-- By default, most tactics work on the goal formula and leave the context
543+-- unchanged. However, most tactics also have a variant that performs a
544+-- similar operation on a statement in the context.
545+
546+-- For example, the tactic "`dsimp at H`" performs simplification on the
547+-- hypothesis `H` in the context.
548+
549+theorem beq_succ (n m : Nat) : (n + 1 == m + 1) = (n == m) :=
550+  decide_eq_decide.mpr Nat.succ_inj
551+
552+theorem succ_inj (n m : Nat) :
553+    n + 1 == m + 1 → n == m := by
554+  intro h
555+  rw [beq_succ] at h
556+  exact h

558+-- Similarly, `apply L at H` matches some conditional statement `L` (of the
559+-- form `X → Y`, say) against a hypothesis `H` in the context. However, unlike
560+-- ordinary `apply` (which rewrites a goal matching `Y` into a subgoal `X`),
561+-- `apply L at H` matches `H` against `X` and, if successful, replaces it with
562+-- `Y`.
563+
564+-- In other words, `apply L at H` gives us a form of "forward reasoning":
565+-- given `X → Y` and a hypothesis matching `X`, it produces a hypothesis
566+-- matching `Y`.
567+
568+-- By contrast, `apply L` is "backward reasoning": it says that if we know
569+-- `X → Y` and we are trying to prove `Y`, it suffices to prove `X`.

776--- The problem is that `m` is already in the context when we invoke
777--- `induction n`. Since `m` is an ordinary argument of the theorem, this is

722+-- The problem is that, at the point where we invoke the induction hypothesis,
723+-- we have already introduced `m` into the context -- intuitively, we have
724+-- told Lean, "Let's consider some particular `n` and `m`..." and we now have
725+-- to prove that, if `double n = double m` for *these particular* `n` and `m`,
726+-- then `n = m`.
727+
728+-- The next tactic, `induction n` says to Lean: We are going to show the goal
729+-- by induction on `n`. That is, we are going to prove, for *all* `n`, that
730+-- the proposition
731+
732+-- - `P n` = "if `double n = double m`, then `n = m`"
733+
734+-- holds, by showing
735+
736+-- - `P 0`
737+
738+--   (i.e., "if `double 0 = double m` then `0 = m`") and
739+
740+-- - `P n → P (.succ n)`
741+
742+--   (i.e., "if `double n = double m` then `n = m`" implies "if
743+--   `double (.succ n) = double m` then `.succ n = m`").
744+
745+-- If we look closely at the second statement, it is saying something rather
746+-- strange: that, for a *particular* `m`, if we know
747+
748+-- - "if `double n = double m` then `n = m`"
749+
750+-- then we can prove
751+
752+-- - "if `double (.succ n) = double m` then `.succ n = m`".
753+
754+-- To see why this is strange, let's think of a particular `m` -- say, `5`.
755+-- The statement is then saying that, if we know
756+
757+-- - `Q` = "if `double n = 10` then `n = 5`"
758+
759+-- then we can prove
760+
761+-- - `R` = "if `double (.succ n) = 10` then `.succ n = 5`".
762+
763+-- But knowing `Q` doesn't give us any help at all with proving `R`! If we
764+-- tried to prove `R` from `Q`, we would start with something like "Suppose
765+-- `double (.succ n) = 10`..." but then we'd be stuck: knowing that
766+-- `double (.succ n)` is `10` tells us nothing helpful about whether
767+-- `double n` is `10` (indeed, it strongly suggests that `double n` is *not*
768+-- `10`!!), so `Q` is useless.
769+
770+-- Trying to carry out this proof by induction on `n` when `m` is already in
771+-- the context doesn't work because we are then trying to prove a statement
772+-- involving *every* `n` but just a *particular* `m`.
773+
774+-- A successful proof of `double_injective` keeps `m` universally quantified
775+-- in the goal statement at the point where the `induction` tactic is invoked
776+-- on `n`.
777+
778+theorem double_injective : ∀ (n m : Nat),
779+    n.double = m.double →
780+    n = m := by
781+  intro n
782+  induction n
783+  case zero =>
784+    rw [Nat.double_zero]
785+    intro m eq
786+    cases m
787+    case zero => rfl
788+    case succ _ =>
789+      rw [Nat.double_succ] at eq
790+      contradiction
791+  case succ n' ih =>
792+  -- Notice that both the goal and the induction hypothesis are
793+  -- different this time: the goal asks us to prove something more
794+  -- general (i.e., we must prove the statement for _every_ `m`), but
795+  -- the induction hypothesis `ih` is correspondingly more flexible,
796+  -- allowing us to choose any `m` we like when we apply it.
797+  intro m eq
798+  -- Now we've introduced the assumption that `double n = double m`.
799+  -- Since we are doing a case analysis on `n`, we also need a case
800+  -- analysis on `m` to keep the two in sync.
801+  cases m
802+  case zero =>
803+    -- The 0 case is trivial:
804+    rw [Nat.double_zero, Nat.double_succ] at eq
805+    contradiction
806+  case succ m' =>
807+    congr
808+    -- Since we are now in the second branch of the `cases m`, the
809+    -- `m'` mentioned in the context is the predecessor of the `m` we
810+    -- started out talking about.  Since we are also in the `succ` branch of
811+    -- the induction, this is perfect: if we instantiate the generic `m`
812+    -- in the IH with the current `m'` (this instantiation is performed
813+    -- automatically by the `apply` in the next step), then `ih` gives
814+    -- us exactly what we need to finish the proof.
815+    apply ih; rw [Nat.double_succ, Nat.double_succ] at eq; injections
816+
817+-- The thing to take away from all this is that you need to be careful, when
818+-- using induction, that you are not trying to prove something too specific:
819+-- When proving a property quantified over variables `n` and `m` by induction
820+-- on `n`, it is sometimes crucial to leave `m` "generic."

875+-- nice: We don't want to have to twist the statements of lemmas to fit the
876+-- needs of a particular strategy for proving them! Rather we want to state

881+-- option for the `induction` tactic does this.

883+theorem double_injective_take2 (n m : Nat) :

868-

870---   `m`, if `(n' + 1).double = m.double` then `n' + 1 = m`. Again there are two
871---   cases to consider for `m`:
872-

914+-- `n`, if `double n = double m` then `n = m`.

917+--   `double n = double m`. We must show that `n = 0`.
918+
919+--   Since `m = 0`, by the definition of `double` we have [double n = 0]. There
920+--   are two cases to consider for `n`. If `n = 0` we are done, since
921+--   `m = 0 = n`, as required. Otherwise, if `n = .succ n'` for some `n'`, we
922+--   derive a contradiction: by the definition of `double`, we can calculate
923+--   `double n = .succ (.succ (double n'))`, but this contradicts the assumption
924+--   that `double n = 0`.
925+
926+-- - Second, suppose `m = .succ m'` and that `n` is again a number such that
927+--   `double n = double m`. We must show that `n = .succ m'`, with the induction
928+--   hypothesis that for every number `s`, if [double s = double m'] then
929+--   `s = m'`.
930+
931+--   By the fact that `m = .succ m'` and the definition of `double`, we have
932+--   `double n = .succ (.succ (double m'))`. There are two cases to consider for
933+--   `n`.
934+
935+--   If `n = 0`, then by definition `double n = 0`, a contradiction.
936+
937+--   Thus, we may assume that `n = .succ n'` for some `n'`, and again by the
938+--   definition of `double` we have
939+--   `.succ (.succ (double n')) = .succ (.succ (double m'))`, which implies by
940+--   injectivity that `double n' = double m'`. Instantiating the induction

943+--   `.succ m' = m`, this is just what we wanted to show. []

929--- `n.double = m.double`, not just `n = m`. When we write
930--- `rw [double_injective n m]`, Lean uses the conclusion `n = m` to rewrite
931--- the goal, and then asks us to prove the hypothesis needed by
932--- `double_injective`. Thus we get two goals: the updated main goal,
933--- `m + p = q`, which follows from `hm`, and the condition from

936--- If we rewrite with a conditional statement of the form `P → a = b`, then
947+-- We'll use a boolean "less or equal" test on numbers, written `n ≤? m` (the
948+-- library function `Nat.ble`), together with the fact that it commutes with
949+-- successor on both sides.
950+
951+infix:52 " ≤? " => Nat.ble
952+
953+theorem zero_ble (m : Nat) : (0 ≤? m) = true := rfl
954+theorem succ_ble_succ (n m : Nat) : ((n + 1) ≤? (m + 1)) = (n ≤? m) := rfl
955+
956+-- Suppose that we want to show that `add` is the inverse of `sub`. Since we
957+-- are working with natural numbers, we need an assumption to prevent `sub`
958+-- from truncating its result. With this assumption, the induction hypothesis
959+-- becomes `forall m, n' ≤? m = true → (m - n') + n' = m`. The beginning of
960+-- the proof uses techniques we have already seen -- in particular, notice how
961+-- we induct on `n` before introducing `m`, so that the induction hypothesis
962+-- becomes sufficiently general.
963+
964+theorem sub_add_ble : ∀ (n m : Nat),
965+    n ≤? m = true → (m - n) + n = m := by
966+  intro n
967+  induction n
968+  case zero =>
969+    intro m h; rw [add_zero]; cases m
970+    case zero => rfl
971+    case succ => rfl
972+  case succ n' ih =>
973+    intro m h; cases m
974+    case zero => contradiction
975+    case succ m' =>
976+      rw [succ_ble_succ] at h
977+      rw [succ_sub_succ, add_succ]
978+    -- At this point, we need to show `(m' - n') + n' + 1 = m' + 1`
979+    -- from the assumption `(n' <= m') = true`.  We could use the
980+    -- `have` tactic to prove `(m' - n') + n' = m'` from the IH.
981+    -- However, we can also just use `rw` directly...
982+      rw [ih]
983+      assumption
984+
985+-- if we rewrite with a conditional statement of the form `P → a = b`, then
937986 -- Lean tries to rewrite with `a = b`, and then asks us to prove `P` in a new
938987 -- subgoal. If the statement has more than one assumption, then we get one
939988 -- subgoal for each assumption.

11181128 -- more powerful *automation* tactics that make Lean help us with low-level
11191129 -- details. But basically we've got what we need to get work done.
11201130 
1121--- Here are the ones we've seen so far.
1122-
1123--- Managing goals and hypotheses:
1124-
1125--- - `intro h`: move an assumption/quantified variable from the goal into the
1126---   local context
1127-
1128--- - `apply thm`: use a theorem, hypothesis, or constructor whose conclusion
1129---   matches the goal; its premises become new goals
1130-
1131--- - `apply thm at h`: use a theorem on a hypothesis in the context, replacing
1132---   `h` by the resulting
1133-
1134---   fact (forward reasoning)
1135-
1136--- - `specialize h ...`: instantiate quantified variables in a hypothesis,
1137---   modifying `h` in place
1138-
1139--- - `replace h := ...`: replace a hypothesis with a newly proved fact
1140-
1141--- - `have h : P := ...`: prove a local fact `P` and add it to the context with
1142---   the name `h`
1143-
1144--- - `contradiction`: close the current goal when the context contains
1145---   contradictory assumptions
1146-
1147--- Equality and rewriting:
1148-
1149--- - `rfl`: close an equality that holds by reflexivity (possibly after
1150---   computation)
1151-
1152--- - `rw [h]`: rewrite the goal using an equality hypothesis or theorem
1153-
1154--- - `rw [h] at h'`: rewrite a hypothesis using an equality hypothesis or
1155---   theorem
1156-
1157--- - `symm`: reverse an equality goal, changing `t = u` to `u = t`
1158-
1159--- - `symm at h`: reverse an equality hypothesis
1160-
1161--- - `calc`: prove a goal about equality or another transitive relation by
1162---   giving a sequence of intermediate steps
1163-
1164--- - `congr`: use congruence to reduce an equality between expressions with the
1165---   same outer form; for example, a goal `f x = f y` may be reduced to `x = y`
1166-
1167--- - `injection h with ...`: use injectivity of constructors to extract
1168---   equalities from constructor applications equations
1169-
1170--- - `injections`: repeatedly use constructor injectivity on suitable equalities
1171---   in the context
1172-
1173--- Simplifying and unfolding definitions:
1174-
1175--- - `dsimp`: simplify definitional computations in the goal
1176--- - `dsimp at h`: simplify definitional computations in a hypothesis
1177-
1178--- Case analysis:
1179-
1180--- - `cases x`: reason separately about the possible constructors of an
1181---   inductively defined value
1182-
1183--- - `cases h : e`: perform case analysis on an expression `e` and add an
1184---   equation named `h` recording the result of the case analysis
1185-
1186--- Induction:
1187-
1188--- - `induction x`: prove the goal by induction on an inductively defined value
1189-
1190--- - `induction x generalizing y`: induction on `x` while generalizing the
1191---   listed local variables, giving a more general induction hypothesis

1131+-- Here are the ones we've seen:

1133+-- - `intro`: move hypotheses/variables from goal to context
1134+
1135+-- - `rfl`: finish the proof (when the goal looks like [e = e])
1136+
1137+-- - `apply`: prove goal using a hypothesis, lemma, or constructor
1138+
1139+-- - `apply... at H`: apply a hypothesis, lemma, or constructor to a hypothesis
1140+--   in the context (forward reasoning)
1141+
1142+-- - `apply... with...`: explicitly specify values for variables that cannot be
1143+--   determined by pattern matching
1144+
1145+-- - `replace h (x:= ...)`: refine a hypothesis by fixing some of its variables
1146+
1147+-- - `dsimp`: simplify computations in the goal
1148+
1149+-- - `dsimp at H`: ... or a hypothesis
1150+
1151+-- - `rw`: use an equality hypothesis (or lemma) to rewrite the goal
1152+
1153+-- - `rw ... at H`: ... or a hypothesis
1154+
1155+-- - `symm`: changes a goal of the form `t=u` into `u=t`
1156+
1157+-- - `symm at H`: changes a hypothesis of the form `t=u` into `u=t`
1158+
1159+-- - `calc`: prove a goal about a transitive relation via a number of
1160+--   intermediate steps
1161+
1162+-- - `unfold`: replace a defined constant by its right-hand side in the goal
1163+
1164+-- - `unfold... at H`: ... or a hypothesis
1165+
1166+-- - `cases ...`: case analysis on values of inductively defined types
1167+
1168+-- - `cases h:...`: specify the name of an equation to be added to the context,
1169+--   recording the result of the case analysis
1170+
1171+-- - `induction ...`: induction on values of inductively defined types
1172+
1173+-- - `induction ... generalizing ...`: hold some variables general while doing
1174+--   induction
1175+
1176+-- - `injection ... with ...`: reason by injectivity on an equality between
1177+--   values of inductively defined types
1178+
1179+-- - `injections ... `: reason by injectivity on all the equalities in the

1181+
1182+-- - `contradiction`: conclude a proof when there's a false hypothesis in the

1184+
1185+-- - `have h : e := ... ` : introduce a "local lemma" `e` and call it `h`
1186+
1187+-- - `congr`: change a goal of the form `f x = f y` into `x = y`

278--- /--
279---   `BEq α` is a typeclass for supplying a boolean-valued equality relation on
280---   `α`, notated as `a == b`. Unlike `DecidableEq α` (which uses `a = b`), this
281---   is `Bool` valued instead of `Prop` valued, and it also does not have any
282---   axioms like being reflexive or agreeing with `=`. It is mainly intended for
283---   programming applications. See `LawfulBEq` for a version that requires that
284---   `==` and `=` coincide.

304+  dsimp [square] at h

412--- Lean's language server can suggest *code actions*, which are small editor
413--- commands that modify the source code. In VS Code, a lightbulb icon appears
414--- on the left when a code action is available at your cursor. You can click
415--- the icon or open the code action menu with `Ctrl + .` on Windows/Linux or
416--- `Command + .` on macOS. For more information, see the [Lean 4 VSCode
417--- extension
418--- manual](https://github.com/leanprover/vscode-lean4/blob/master/vscode-lean4/manual/manual.md#code-actions).
419-
420--- Some code actions can generate the explicit branches needed for pattern
421--- matching. This is especially useful when working with `match` expressions,
422--- or with tactics such as `cases` and `induction`, which we saw in previous
423--- chapters.
